title: Advanced Git
tagline: The tools you reach for once a week, not once a day -- but genuinely painful to not know when you need them.

concept.label: What
concept.text: git stash (shelve uncommitted work), git cherry-pick (copy one commit elsewhere), .gitignore, tags, and hooks.

concept.label: Why
concept.text: Real projects hit situations none of Modules 1-8 alone solve: switching branches mid-work, needing ONE commit from another branch, keeping secrets out of history.

concept.label: How
concept.text: git stash / stash pop; git cherry-pick <hash>; a .gitignore file listing patterns to never track; git tag v1.0 for release points.

concept.label: When
concept.text: Stash: switching branches with unfinished work. Cherry-pick: a fix belongs on two branches. .gitignore: before your FIRST commit, ideally.

concept.label: Where
concept.text: The toolbox every experienced Git user has reached for, even if rarely.

mnemonic.label: S.C.G.T.
mnemonic.text: Stash (shelve) · Cherry-pick (copy one commit) · .Gitignore (exclude) · Tag (mark a release)

sandboxNote.text: practice these on your existing Module 1-7 repo -- it already has enough branches and history to make all four genuinely useful.

code:
echo "node_modules/" > .gitignore   # GITIGNORE: never track these, ever
echo "*.log" >> .gitignore
git add .gitignore && git commit -m "Add gitignore"

echo "unfinished work" >> README.md
git stash                        # STASH: shelve this mess without committing it
git switch main                  # clean switch -- the mess came off your working dir
git switch -                     # back to where you were
git stash pop                    # bring the shelved work back

git switch main
git log --oneline other-branch   # find a commit hash on another branch you need HERE
git cherry-pick a1b2c3d           # CHERRY-PICK: copy just that one commit onto main

git tag v1.0.0                    # TAG: mark this exact commit as a named release
git push origin v1.0.0             # tags need pushing separately from commits

cycle.title: Read the concept table once
cycle.text: These four solve four DIFFERENT problems -- don't try to memorise them as one topic. Stash is about time (later), cherry-pick is about space (another branch), .gitignore is about exclusion, tags are about naming a point in history.

cycle.title: Type the code yourself — no copy-paste
cycle.text: Do all four for real. For stash specifically: start genuinely unfinished work, get interrupted (switch branches for something else), and use stash exactly as you would in a real interruption.
cycle.hint: git stash list shows everything you've shelved -- it's easy to forget a stash exists. Check it occasionally so old shelved work doesn't just vanish from memory.

cycle.title: Apply it to your own data
cycle.text: Create a real .gitignore for a project type you actually use (Python, Node, etc. -- GitHub's own gitignore templates are a good reference), and cherry-pick one real commit between two of your own branches.

cycle.title: Reflect & note
cycle.text: Which of the four solved a real annoyance you'd already hit before knowing the fix existed?
cycle.placeholder: e.g. I'd been manually copy-pasting a bugfix between two branches for weeks before learning cherry-pick existed -- one command replaced that entire manual process...

cycle.title: Tick off before moving on
checklist: I can describe what each of stash/cherry-pick/.gitignore/tag solves.
I used git stash and stash pop during a real interruption.
I cherry-picked a real commit from one branch onto another.
I wrote a real .gitignore and tagged a release with git tag.
I wrote a reflection note above.

closingQuote: \u201cEvery Git GUI, every GitHub button, every IDE integration is a thin layer over the exact commands in these nine modules. Learn the commands once, and every tool built on top of them makes sense immediately.\u201d
